title: Ranked-Choice Voting: The Math That Kills the Spoiler Effect
subtitle: How letting voters rank candidates instead of picking one changes who wins — and the trade-offs no voting system can escape.
hook: In a normal election you pick one candidate. Simple — but it has a famous flaw: a third candidate you love can 'split the vote' and hand victory to the one you like *least*. This is the **spoiler effect**, and it quietly shapes how people vote (and which candidates even run). **Ranked-choice voting** tries to fix it by asking a different question: not "who's your favorite?" but "rank them in order." That small change has surprisingly deep consequences.

sections.heading: The problem with picking just one
sections.body: Under **first-past-the-post** (pick one, most votes wins), imagine 45% back candidate A, while 55% lean progressive but split 30/25 between B and C. The majority prefers *either* B or C over A — yet A wins with only 45%, because the 55% divided itself. Voters learn this and start voting *strategically*, abandoning their true favorite for the 'lesser evil' who can actually win. That pressure is exactly what ranked-choice is designed to relieve.

sections.heading: How the count works (instant-runoff)
items: Voters **rank** candidates: 1st choice, 2nd choice, 3rd, and so on.
Count everyone's **1st choices**. If a candidate has a **majority (>50%)**, they win — done.
If not, **eliminate the last-place candidate** and look at those ballots' *next* choice.
**Redistribute** those votes to the surviving candidates and re-count.
Repeat — eliminating and redistributing — until someone crosses 50%.

sections.caption: Instant-runoff in one picture: no majority triggers elimination of the lowest candidate, whose ballots flow to their next choice, and the count repeats.

sections.label: What it changes
sections.body: Because a candidate needs broad support to reach 50%, they benefit from being lots of voters' *second* choice, not just firing up a narrow base. In theory this rewards coalition-building and lets you rank your true favorite first without 'wasting' your vote — the spoiler pressure eases. Cities like San Francisco and states like Maine and Alaska now use it for real elections.

sections.heading: The honest trade-offs
sections.body:
Ranked-choice is not a free lunch, and supporters and critics disagree sharply. Critics point to **non-monotonicity** — in rare cases, ranking a candidate *higher* can actually cause them to lose — and to real-world confusion, longer ballot-counting, and higher rates of spoiled ballots. Supporters counter that it elects more broadly-acceptable winners and reduces negative campaigning, and that the edge cases are rare in practice.

Underneath it all sits a deeper result: **Arrow's Impossibility Theorem** proved that no ranked voting system can satisfy every reasonable fairness criterion at once. So the real debate isn't 'which system is perfect' but 'which set of trade-offs do we prefer' — a genuinely open question that reasonable people land on differently.

takeaways: First-past-the-post suffers the **spoiler effect**: splitting votes can elect the least-preferred candidate.
Ranked-choice (instant-runoff) has voters **rank** candidates instead of picking one.
Counting **eliminates the last-place candidate and redistributes** their ballots until someone passes 50%.
It can ease spoiler pressure and reward broad appeal; used in Maine, Alaska, and cities like SF.
Trade-offs are real (non-monotonicity, complexity) — and **Arrow's theorem** says no system is flawless.
